acromuseum.text: Outside the entrance, on the glass floor of the forecourt, looking down.
This museum was built for one job: to hold everything found on the Acropolis rock and its slopes. It opened in June 2009, and today it shows more than 4,250 objects.

Look down through the glass. The whole building stands on pillars above an excavated neighbourhood, with houses and workshops from classical and early Byzantine times. Parts of the floor inside are glass too.
Inside, at the foot of the long sloping gallery.

This first gallery slopes upward on purpose, like the climb up to the rock. Then comes a big hall of archaic finds, and pieces from the Erechtheion, the temple of Athena Nike and the gateway you may have walked through.
Look out for the Maidens, the Caryatids from the Erechtheion. One of them ended up in the British Museum in London.
On the top floor, at the north windows, with the Parthenon in view.
This top floor is the heart of the museum. Notice it sits at an angle to the rest of the building. That's so it lines up with the Parthenon itself. Look out the north windows and there it is.
The 48 columns in this hall mark out the outline of the temple, and the sculptures face outward, the way they did on the building.

Now look closely at the sculptures. Where Parthenon pieces are missing, the museum shows casts in their place. Many of the missing pieces are in London. Between 1801 and 1812, agents of Lord Elgin took about half the surviving Parthenon sculptures.
Whether that was legal is still disputed. A British inquiry in 1816 said it was. In 1983 Greece formally asked Britain to return them, and Greek officials hope this room will help bring them home.
Not everyone loves the display. Some archaeologists and museum professionals criticise the lighting and the politics of the design. Decide for yourself.

acropolis.text: Stand just past the ticket gate at the west entrance, to the side of the path, where you can look up at the gateway of columns.
Here we are, at the foot of the Acropolis. Take a breath before the climb.

Almost everything you'll see up top was built in one burst of confidence. In 480 BC the Persians sacked Athens and destroyed the temples on this hill. After the Greeks won that war, the city rebuilt it all under the statesman Pericles.
Two practical things before we climb. Take the marble steps slowly and watch your footing. And carry water with you.
Stop inside the gateway, between the big columns.
This gateway is the Propylaia, designed by the architect Mnesikles and built from 437 to 432 BC.
Here's something most people walk straight past. The Propylaia was never finished. Work stopped in 432 BC, with the builders' lifting bosses still left on the blocks.

Look up to your right at the little temple on its own bastion. That's the temple of Athena Nike, Athena of Victory, the smallest temple on the hill. Its date isn't settled: UNESCO gives 427 to 424 BC, other sources say it was finished around 420 BC.
Walk through the gateway onto the open rock and stop where you see the west end of the Parthenon at an angle.

And there it is. The Parthenon, the temple of Athena, protector of the city. It was begun in 447 BC and completed in 438 BC, with the carving going on until 432. The architects were Iktinos and Kallikrates, and the sculptor Pheidias was in charge of the sculpture.

Now here's the secret of this building. It looks perfectly straight, but it isn't. The floor bulges upward in the middle, about 10 centimetres over 70 metres. The columns swell slightly too. Scholars still argue about exactly why the builders did it.

Picture it whole. Inside stood the statue of Athena by Pheidias, in gold and ivory. According to the historian Thucydides, Pericles told the Athenians it held forty talents of pure gold, a reserve the city could use in an emergency.
Stay beside the Parthenon, anywhere along its long side.

Here's the part of the story most visitors never hear. For a very long time this was a church. It became a church, first of Saint Sophia, Holy Wisdom, and later of the Virgin Mary. The Greek Ministry of Culture says that happened in the fifth century AD; other sources say the late 500s, so the sources differ. Medieval Greeks called it the church of the Theotokos Atheniotissa, Our Lady of Athens.

Then came Latin crusader lords, and for about 250 years it was a Catholic church of Our Lady. The Ottomans took the hill in 1458, or 1460 by another account, and before the end of that century the Parthenon was a mosque. Exactly how that happened is unclear.

Then came the worst day in its history. On 26 September 1687 a Venetian army was bombarding the hill. The Ottomans were storing gunpowder inside the Parthenon. A mortar round hit, and the middle of the building blew apart. Accounts from the time disagree on whether the gunners meant to hit it.

More was lost later. From 1801 to 1812, agents of the British ambassador, Lord Elgin, removed about half the surviving sculptures and sent them to Britain. Whether that was legal is still disputed, and Greece has asked for them back.
The cranes you see are the restoration teams. Their current work began in 1975, and it's still going.
Cross to the north side and face the porch held up by six statues of young women.
This is the Erechtheion, and these are the Maidens, the Caryatids, carrying the roof on their heads. One of the original Maidens ended up in the British Museum in London.

This is also where Athens kept its founding legend. As the story goes, Athena and Poseidon competed for the city, a contest carved on the west end of the Parthenon. It's legend, not history, but Athenians pointed to a sacred olive of Athena here, and to marks in the rock said to be from Poseidon's trident.
On your way back down, at the top of the gateway steps.

Take one last look back. A temple, a treasury, a church of the Virgin Mary, a mosque, a gunpowder store, then a ruin, and now a building that people are patiently putting back together. Every age has found something here worth saving.

Below the entrance is a bare rocky hill, the Areopagus. The book of Acts links it to the apostle Paul's speech to the Athenians, although historians aren't sure whether he spoke on the hill itself or before the council named after it.

agora.text: Just inside the entrance, where you can see the long two-storey colonnade to your left and the temple on the hill to your right.

Welcome to the Agora, the heart of ancient Athens. It was the business, political and legal centre of the city, where citizens and foreigners, litigants and jurors, merchants and philosophers all met, in one open space below the Acropolis.
Picture it crowded. In the 400s and 300s BC there were women running inns and selling goods here, alongside everyone else.
On the west side stood the Monument of the Eponymous Heroes. It worked as the city's notice board, where new laws, public events and military call-ups were posted.
This is also the market where, according to Acts chapter seventeen, the apostle Paul argued daily with anyone who would listen.
Walk up Market Hill and stop at the corner of the temple.

This is one of the best-preserved Greek temples anywhere, still standing largely intact. It honours Hephaestus, god of fire and metalwork, and fittingly, potters and metalworkers had their shops all around it. Work began in 449 BC.
For a long time people called it the Theseion, thinking the hero Theseus was buried here. That was a mistake. Inscriptions found inside tie it firmly to Hephaestus.
Why did it survive when so much else fell? It kept being used. It became a church of Saint George, probably around AD 700, although nobody knows exactly when, and it stayed a church until 1834.
At the foot of the long two-storey building on the east side.
This long building is a gift. King Attalos the Second of Pergamon had studied in Athens and paid for it as a thank-you. Behind the colonnade were rows of rooms used as shops.
Invaders called the Heruli burned its woodwork in AD 267. What you see now was rebuilt from 1952 to 1956 by the American School of Classical Studies, which has been digging here since 1931.

Inside is the Agora museum, and most of it is about the birth of democracy. A good place to end: in the square where Athenians argued, voted and traded, a few steps from where the first citizens tried to govern themselves.

areopagus.text: On a flat spot near the top of the rock, well back from the edges, facing the Acropolis gateway.
This bare, rocky hill is the Areopagus. The name means the Hill of Ares, the god of war. In the King James Bible it's Mars' hill.
Watch your footing up here. The rock is uneven, and there are no railings at the edges.

Long before Paul, this rock was famous for justice. The council that met here became the court of Athens for murder and certain religious crimes. Exactly how early that began, historians aren't sure, but it may go back to the 7th century BC.

The Athenians liked a good origin story. Myth said the war god Ares himself was put on trial here by the other gods. And in the play The Eumenides, from 458 BC, the playwright Aeschylus set the trial of Orestes on this hill.

Now to the apostle Paul. The book of Acts, chapter seventeen, tells how the apostle Paul waited in Athens, and his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry. He argued daily in the synagogue, and in the market below us.

Some of the philosophers brought him unto Areopagus, Acts says, to explain his new teaching. Here historians aren't sure what that means: this hill itself, or the council named after it, which by Paul's time probably met down in the marketplace instead. One scholar has even suggested the hearing may have been part lecture, part trial.

Here are his opening words, in the King James Version: "Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious. For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, to the unknown god. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you."
Picture saying this in a city Acts describes as wholly given to idolatry: that God that made the world dwelleth not in temples made with hands.
He even quoted their own Greek poets back to them. It was a sermon built for this audience.
Turn to look down over the Agora.

Acts is honest about the result. When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, and others said they would hear him again. But a few believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris.
Paul did not win the crowd that day. But a few people listened, and the words Acts records have been read all over the world ever since.

lycabettus.text: At the start of the path or the funicular station on Aristippou Street.

Lycabettus is the highest point in central Athens, 277 metres above sea level. You can ride the funicular from Aristippou Street in Kolonaki, or walk the paved path, which Wikivoyage reckons takes about 30 minutes.
If you walk, you'll climb through pines that cover the lower slopes of this big limestone hill.
On the terrace beside the small white chapel, looking southwest toward the Acropolis.
Here's your reward. Take a moment to look out over the city and find the Acropolis.
Up here are the little Chapel of Saint George, from the 1800s, a restaurant, and just below, an open-air theatre that reopened in September 2023 after 15 years closed.

And the name? It may come from the Greek word for wolf, from a time when wolves roamed here, or from an older, pre-Greek word. Nobody's sure. There's a myth too: Athena was carrying a mountain to build up the Acropolis, dropped it, and here it is.
Stay for sunset if you can, and then watch the city lights come on.

metropolis.text: In Mitropoleos Square, facing the cathedral's front.
This is the Metropolitan Cathedral of the Annunciation, the cathedral of the Archbishop of Athens and all Greece. King Otto and Queen Amalia laid its first stone on Christmas Day 1842.
It wasn't quick. It took several architects and 20 years, and builders used marble from 72 demolished churches. It was dedicated in May 1862.

Inside lie two people Greeks hold very dear. Saint Philothei, martyred in 1589, remembered for buying the freedom of Greek women enslaved under Ottoman rule. And Patriarch Gregory the Fifth, hanged in 1821 in revenge for the Greek uprising. Greek sailors rescued his body, and eventually it was enshrined here in Athens.
If a service is on, step in quietly. A good rule of thumb for Greek churches: no short sleeves or bare legs, as a mark of respect.
Walk to the small stone church just south of the cathedral.
Now look at this little church beside the giant. It's Saint Eleftherios, nicknamed the Little Metropolis.
We don't yet have a source we trust for its history, so we won't guess. It's well worth a slow walk around the outside.
In the square, the two statues are Constantine the Eleventh, the last Byzantine emperor, and Archbishop Damaskinos, who led the church in Athens through the Second World War.

monastiraki.text: In the middle of Monastiraki Square, by the metro entrance, with the small church in front of you and the Acropolis rising behind the rooftops.

Welcome to Monastiraki, the little monastery. The name comes from that small church in the square, the Pantanassa. It was the main church of a monastery that has since vanished. The encyclopedia dates it to the 900s AD; we haven't found a second source to confirm that.
Its monastery was once called the Great Monastery. Later it became the little monastery, and that name spread to the whole neighbourhood.
Today it's a flea market district and one of the main places to shop in Athens: antiques, souvenirs, crafts and plenty of oddities. Keep your bag zipped in the crowds.
Turn to face the building with the dome and the arched porch on the square.

That domed building is the Tzistarakis Mosque, built in 1759 by the Ottoman governor of Athens. Our source lists it as part of the Museum of Greek Folk Art, with a pottery collection inside, but that may be out of date. Check whether it's open before you plan to go in.

It comes with a dark story. An inscription at the Temple of Olympian Zeus records a column pulled down there in 1759, and a chronicler blamed this governor, who wanted marble to make lime for his mosque. Another account says the column came from Hadrian's Library next door instead. Either way, tradition says he was dismissed for sacrilege, and when plague broke out later that year, some Athenians said it was the price.
After independence it changed roles many times. In March 1834 it even hosted a ball for the new king, Otto.
Walk a few steps behind the mosque to the railings along the line of tall columns.
Behind the mosque, those columns are the front of Hadrian's Library, built by the emperor Hadrian in AD 132.

Picture the inside: shelves of papyrus rolls, reading rooms, lecture halls in the corners, gilded wooden ceilings and marble walls. Invaders wrecked it in 267, and later three churches were built inside the ruins.
Monastiraki is easy to reach and easy to leave. The metro station right on the square serves Lines 1 and 3.

olympieion.text: On the pavement beside the marble arch, well back from the kerb of busy Amalias Avenue.
This marble gateway is Hadrian's Arch. Over the opening, on each side, a line of Greek is carved. On the side facing the Acropolis, it says: this is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus.

The other side, facing the temple, says: this is the city of Hadrian, and not of Theseus. Quite a compliment to a Roman emperor. Nobody knows for certain who put the arch up, but it was probably the citizens of Athens.
Historians aren't sure what the words mean: the whole city, or an old part and a new part. The arch itself was probably put up to honour Hadrian around AD 131 or 132.
Inside the site, at the end of the path where the tall columns stand in a group.
Now look at those giant columns. This was meant to be the greatest temple in the ancient world, for Zeus, king of the gods. Its story is one of the great builders' sagas.

Around 550 BC the tyrant Peisistratus built a temple here, and around 520 BC his sons started this enormous one. Then it stalled. Only the platform and parts of the columns were done, and it sat that way for 336 years. In 174 BC a Greek king, Antiochus the Fourth, restarted the work, until his death in 164 BC stopped it again. Then the Roman general Sulla carried off some of the unfinished columns to Rome.

Finally the emperor Hadrian finished it and dedicated it in AD 132, more than six centuries after it was started. It had 104 columns, each about 17 metres tall, the largest temple in Greece. Inside stood a gold-and-ivory Zeus, and next to the god, a statue of Hadrian himself.
Stand where you can see the single column lying on the ground in pieces.
So where did 104 columns go? By 1436 a traveller counted only 21 standing. Over the centuries the marble was simply taken.

One loss is written on the stone itself. An inscription on a surviving column records that on 27 April 1759 a column was pulled down. A chronicler blamed the Ottoman governor, Tzistarakis, who wanted marble for plaster for his new mosque. Another account says it was more likely a column from Hadrian's Library. Either way, his mosque still stands in Monastiraki.
Fifteen columns stand today. The one lying in pieces at your feet came down in a storm in 1852. It's the clearest sense you'll get of just how huge they are.

plaka.text: On Adrianou Street, any spot where you can see the Acropolis rock above the rooftops.

This is Plaka, the old neighbourhood wrapped around the slopes below the Acropolis. People call it the Neighbourhood of the Gods. It's the oldest district in Athens, with people living here since the Stone Age. Even so, it was briefly emptied during the battles of 1826, in the War of Independence.
You're walking on very old lines. Some of these streets, this one, Adrianou, among them, follow routes that go back to ancient times.

Even the name is a small mystery. Some say Plaka comes from words meaning old Athens in the language of Albanian settlers, who lived here in large numbers until the late 1800s. Others say it's from a stone plaque that once marked a crossroads. Nobody knows for sure.
In 1884 a fire burned a large part of the neighbourhood. Archaeologists used the gap to dig at the Roman Agora and Hadrian's Library.
One more detail. According to the encyclopedia, Plaka's power, water and phone lines all run in tunnels underground, and it's the only Athens neighbourhood done that way.
From Stratonos Street, take the narrow lanes up toward the Acropolis rock. The steps are steep and uneven.

Suddenly you're on a Greek island. This is Anafiotika. In the time of King Otto, builders from the island of Anafi came to work on the new royal palace, and they built themselves homes here the way they did back home.
Small white cube houses, steps that end at little terraces, and dead ends everywhere. Refugees from Asia Minor joined them in 1922.
Only 45 houses are left. The lanes have no names, and the houses go by numbers.
People live in these houses, so keep your voice down.
Find a terrace, look out over the city, and catch your breath. This is one of the quietest corners in the centre of Athens.

syntagma.text: At the top of the marble steps on the east side of the square, facing the big pale building across the avenue.
This is Syntagma, which means Constitution. The square is named for the constitution the first king of Greece, Otto, was forced to grant after an uprising on 3 September 1843.

The building across the road was Otto's palace, designed by the Bavarian architect Friedrich von Gärtner, and begun in 1836. In 1929 the government decided it would house Parliament for good, and the Senate first met there in 1934. The Parliament isn't open to visitors, but the National Gardens beside it are.
Cross at the lights and stand at the edge of the open space in front of the Parliament, facing the carved wall with the guards. Stay behind any barrier.

The carved wall is the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a memorial for every Greek soldier killed in war. The sculptor Fokion Rok carved a fallen soldier lying on the ground, and it was unveiled on 25 March 1932.

The guards are Evzones, from the Presidential Guard, the last Evzone unit in the Greek army. Watch them. They hold perfectly still, and every fifteen minutes they swap places in slow, highly stylised moves. A changeover happens every hour on the hour.

The uniform comes from the fighters of the War of Independence. On most days the guards wear a long tunic, navy blue in winter and light khaki in summer. On Sundays and holidays they wear the white kilt, the fustanella, made from 30 metres of cloth. Tradition says it has 400 pleats, one for each year of Ottoman rule. And those red clogs with the black pompoms weigh around 1.5 kilos each.
On Sunday mornings at 11 there's the Grand Change, with the whole guard, its officers and a military band.
Please don't touch the guards or step into their path. They are on duty at a war memorial.
